title: CLOPS: Benchmarking System Speed at Utility Scale
abstract: As quantum processors scale to hundreds of qubits, execution speed is a critical performance dimension alongside scale and quality. While substantial progress has been made in benchmarking circuit fidelity, existing speed metrics often fail to reflect the sustained, end-to-end throughput experienced by users running utility-scale workloads. This shortfall is especially pronounced for layered, parameterized circuits executed repeatedly within classical-quantum workflows, such as variational algorithms and error-mitigated simulations.   In this work, we formalize CLOPS_h (Circuit Layer Operations Per Second) as a holistic speed benchmark defined over layered, hardware-aware circuits. CLOPS_h measures the sustained rate at which the system executes physical layers, parallel slices of qubit-disjoint two-qubit gates separated by synchronization barriers. Because each such layer is one time slice of an N-qubit circuit, this rate maps directly to the execution rate of layered $N$-qubit circuits, connecting CLOPS_h to published device capability claims, and to the device-level throughput ceiling we formalize as Max Circuits Per Second (MCPS). CLOPS_h is obtained under layer-fidelity operating conditions, binding the speed measurement to an independently verified quality envelope, and it shares its layer decomposition with scalable layer-fidelity (LF) quality benchmarks, enabling coherent interpretation of speed and quality without conflating the two.
summary: This paper introduces CLOPSh, a new benchmark metric designed to accurately measure the sustained operational speed of large-scale quantum processors. It addresses the gap in current metrics by defining speed based on layered, hardware-aware circuits, ensuring that speed measurements are intrinsically linked to independently verified quality levels. This provides a necessary, holistic tool for assessing the true utility potential of quantum hardware.
main_problem: Existing quantum speed metrics fail to capture the sustained, end-to-end throughput required for utility-scale quantum algorithms, especially those involving classical-quantum feedback loops.
main_result: The authors propose CLOPSh (Circuit Layer Operations Per Second), a holistic benchmark that measures sustained throughput by defining speed over hardware-aware, layered circuits, thereby linking speed directly to independently verified quality envelopes.
method: The work formalizes a new benchmarking metric, CLOPSh, which measures the rate of executing physical circuit layers, ensuring the speed measurement is structurally compatible with existing Layer Fidelity (LF) quality benchmarks.
model_or_system: The focus is on scaling quantum processors to hundreds of qubits, analyzing performance across an abstraction hierarchy (Qubit $ightarrow$ Device $ightarrow$ System $ightarrow$ Application) to address utility-scale workloads.
key_observables: CLOPSh (Circuit Layer Operations Per Second), Max Circuits Per Second (MCPS), Layer Fidelity (LF), and the overall system throughput rate.
important_parameters: Utility-scale workloads, layered/parameterized circuits, and the need to account for classical-quantum overheads.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that sustained, steady-state throughput, measured layer-by-layer, is the correct metric to guide hardware development beyond simple gate counts or fidelity measurements.
figures_summary: The notes mention a table organizing representative benchmarks across four levels of abstraction (Qubit, Device, System, Application) for Scale, Quality, and Speed, and a figure illustrating physical sublayers as the counting unit for CLOPSh.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the limitations of existing metrics (QV, gate rates), introduces the comprehensive CLOPS framework, and then details CLOPSh as the specific, necessary instantiation for the utility-scale regime, ensuring speed and quality are measured coherently.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, multi-level framework for benchmarking quantum hardware performance, which is crucial for any theoretical work relying on realistic estimates of quantum computation time or resource scaling.
